title: Night recorder log from the Orra Pass
public_context: Acoustic field surveys use microphones to record calls that may be difficult to observe directly. A detection depends on both animal activity and recording conditions, including noise, placement, and the time window chosen for analysis. Repeated recordings can reveal patterns while still leaving movement and abundance uncertain.
source_text:
Four autonomous recorders were placed along the Orra Pass footpath from 3 to 18 June to document the dusk calls of the slate-throated tree cricket. The units were spaced between 180 and 240 metres apart, with microphones fixed at roughly chest height on numbered stakes. The western pair faced a windbreak; the eastern pair faced an open drainage cut. A maintenance note says the team chose those positions to keep the units above the seasonal seep, not to represent equal habitat areas.

The analysis counted a call bout when at least three pulses appeared within a two-second interval. Each file was divided into ten-minute windows, and the first twenty minutes after sunset were excluded because footpath users frequently passed during that period. Across the remaining window, detections rose at the two eastern units on 9 and 10 June. The western units did not show the same increase, although their microphone housings collected more wind noise on both nights.

A ranger's notebook records that a drainage crew cleared brush from the eastern cut on 8 June. The survey authors say the clearing may have made calls easier to receive, but they did not measure sound transmission before and after the work. They also note that the rain gauge registered a brief shower on the 9th, while the closest weather station is several kilometres away. Neither observation is treated as a direct count of animals.

The team did not interpret a quiet recorder as evidence that the species was absent from the surrounding slope. A unit can miss calls outside its microphone's reach, and the pass has no continuous coverage between stakes. Nor did the report count each pulse as a separate animal; a single calling individual can produce many bouts. The authors used the word detection for a file window meeting the pulse rule, not for a confirmed location or a known number of crickets.

On 12 June, staff moved the westernmost unit two metres after discovering that its stake leaned into a branch. The move was logged, and the before-and-after recordings were not pooled in the placement comparison. A small hand-listening review agreed with most machine flags but rejected several windows containing a metal gate rattle. The summary recommends another season with paired microphones near the drainage cut and windbreak, plus a short calibration recording before dusk. It does not state whether the eastern increase reflected more callers, clearer transmission, or both.
authoring_note: This dossier treats acoustic detection as a window-level measurement affected by coverage and transmission, with a maintenance event and a non-pooled placement change.

supported_claims.claim: Four recorders surveyed slate-throated tree cricket calls along the Orra Pass during 3–18 June.
evidence: Four autonomous recorders were placed along the Orra Pass footpath from 3 to 18 June to document the dusk calls of the slate-throated tree cricket.

supported_claims.claim: The analysis defined a call bout using a pulse threshold and divided files into ten-minute windows.
evidence: The analysis counted a call bout when at least three pulses appeared within a two-second interval. Each file was divided into ten-minute windows, and the first twenty minutes after sunset were excluded because footpath users frequently passed during that period.

supported_claims.claim: Eastern unit detections rose on 9 and 10 June while western units did not show the same rise.
evidence: Across the remaining window, detections rose at the two eastern units on 9 and 10 June. The western units did not show the same increase, although their microphone housings collected more wind noise on both nights.

supported_claims.claim: A ranger recorded eastern brush clearing on 8 June, which authors say may have improved call reception without measuring transmission change.
evidence: A ranger's notebook records that a drainage crew cleared brush from the eastern cut on 8 June. The survey authors say the clearing may have made calls easier to receive, but they did not measure sound transmission before and after the work.

supported_claims.claim: The westernmost recorder moved two metres on 12 June and those recordings were excluded from the placement comparison.
evidence: On 12 June, staff moved the westernmost unit two metres after discovering that its stake leaned into a branch. The move was logged, and the before-and-after recordings were not pooled in the placement comparison.

supported_claims.claim: The summary leaves caller abundance and transmission change as unresolved alternatives for the eastern increase.
evidence: It does not state whether the eastern increase reflected more callers, clearer transmission, or both.

explicit_negatives.claim: A quiet recorder was not treated as proof of species absence from the surrounding slope.
evidence: The team did not interpret a quiet recorder as evidence that the species was absent from the surrounding slope.

explicit_negatives.claim: The report did not treat each pulse as a separate animal.
evidence: Nor did the report count each pulse as a separate animal; a single calling individual can produce many bouts.

licensed_inferences.claim: The eastern rise is compatible with a change in audibility after brush clearing, but the survey cannot distinguish that account from a change in calling activity.
licensed_inferences.rationale: The detections rose after the recorded clearing and the authors explicitly leave clearer transmission and more callers open; no before-and-after transmission measure resolves them.

licensed_inferences.claim: The placement comparison should be interpreted with caution because positions had different surroundings and the west unit changed position during the survey.
licensed_inferences.rationale: The recorder locations faced different site features, and one west recording sequence was excluded from pooling after a documented move.

unspecified_probes.neutral_question: Which recorder model was used at the eastern drainage cut?
unspecified_probes.presupposition_question: Was the eastern drainage-cut recording made with a Cedarline R4 recorder?
unspecified_probes.candidate_claim: A Cedarline R4 recorder was used at the eastern drainage cut.
unspecified_probes.boundary_note: The summary describes autonomous units but gives no make or model; neither the proposed model nor its negation follows.

unspecified_probes.neutral_question: What was the air temperature beside the eastern units on 10 June?
unspecified_probes.presupposition_question: Was the air temperature beside both eastern units 17 degrees on 10 June?
unspecified_probes.candidate_claim: The air temperature beside both eastern units was 17 degrees on 10 June.
unspecified_probes.boundary_note: The nearest station is described as distant, but the report supplies no local temperature reading.

unspecified_probes.neutral_question: What accounts for the eastern detection rise after brush clearing, if anything?
unspecified_probes.presupposition_question: Was the full eastern increase due solely to improved audibility after brush clearing?
unspecified_probes.candidate_claim: The full eastern detection increase was due solely to improved audibility after brush clearing.
unspecified_probes.boundary_note: The authors leave more callers, clearer transmission, or both open; they do not rule out an audibility-only account or establish it.

consistency_questions.question: How does the brush-clearing note affect interpretation of the eastern detection rise?
consistency_questions.reference_answer: The timing makes improved reception plausible, but the lack of transmission measurements leaves increased calling activity or a combination possible.

consistency_questions.question: What do the pulse rule and quiet-recorder caveat allow a reader to conclude about abundance or absence?
consistency_questions.reference_answer: The rule counts qualifying bouts in windows; it does not count individual animals, and a quiet unit cannot establish absence beyond its limited coverage.
